newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korean economy seen bottoming out mid-1997.
newsitem.headline: South Korean economy seen bottoming out mid-1997.

text.p: Despite a central bank forecast of a further slowdown, the South Korean economy is expected to turn around by the middle of 1997, private economists said at the weekend.
A strengthening yen and an expected pick-up of the world memory chip industry next year would stop the economy's downward trend, they said.
"I see the current cycle reaching its bottom by the middle of 1997 and then improving, though slowly," said Lee Youn-ho, chief executive of the LG Economic Research Institute.
Lee's projection came shortly after the central Bank of Korea on Friday presented gloomy economic forercasts for 1997.
The bank said next year's gross domestic product was expected to slow to 6.4 percent from an estimated 6.9 percent rise this year. The economy grew by 9.0 percent in 1995.
Many economic analysts foresaw the yen rebounding to around 105 to the dollar by late 1997 from around 113 yen at present and the slump in the global semiconductor market bottoming out by that time.
The weak yen has made Japanese products cheaper, wiping out the price competitiveness that South Korean exports had enjoyed in export markets against Japanese products.

"The yen will likely regain strength while the won has room to go down further. This means our exports will be given a chance to recover competitiveness," said Ohn Ki-un, economist at the Korea Institute for International Economics and Trade.
The expected recovery of world trade volume over the next few years would also help boost South Korean exports, engine for the nation's economic growth, analysts said.
"World trade volume is seen growing by about six percent next year after an estimated five percent rise this year. The pace will later accelerate," said Ohn.
Ohn and many other analysts say South Korea's annual GDP growth is seen recovering from 1998 and stabilising at between 6.5 percent and 7.0 percent until 2000.
"I think the stable 6.5-7.0 percent range would be quite sound for our economy. In broader terms, the economy is still on an acceptable course," said Ohn.
Analysts said the the global memory chip industry would begin widely using 64-megabit dynamic random access memory (DRAM) chips from early 1998, upgrading from 16-megabit ones widely used now.
"Korean chip makers will be able to take the competitive edge in 64-megabit DRAM production and the changing demand will help them," said Dongwon Securities' Jeon Woo-jong.

This year's plunge in 16-megabit DRAM prices by about 80 percent has been cited as the biggest single factor dampening South Korean exports. Semiconductors make up about 20 percent of the nation's exports.
Government data showed semiconductor exports fell 14.5 percent to $15 billion for the first 10 months of this year from $17.5 billion for the same 10-month period in 1995.
The U.S. Semiconductor Industry Association earlier said the world semiconductor market would return to double-digit growth in 1998 and 1999 after a slim 7.4 percent growth in 1997.
The Bank of Korea forecast next year's current account deficit at $18 billion, down slightly from an estimated $22 billion shortfall this year. Last year, the shortfall was $8.95 billion.
